Some time after the advent of the Rule of the Seven, a young man by the name of Hytia came before the court, bringing with him the lost Ark of the Covenant. He claimed to be a bastard son of Sûrya — one of many — raised in secret by the fallen general Esato. Though he had been raised in poverty and thievery on the streets of Angereb after his mother's passing and the general's murder, he had never forgotten the duties of his blood, and had deployed great cunning and skill in stealing the Ark from the Kashta on the night of the sacking of Taborime. For this mighty deed, Hytia was proclaimed a hero by the Court of Seven, and given the province of Angereb to rule as his own. His was a compassionate rule, for he knew well the suffering of the people, having long been one of their own, and abolished many of the oppressive traditions against craftsmen and traders. Thus did Angereb grow to be a place of trade and riches, renowned throughout Enbesa. Hytia, too, was much-loved by all in Angereb, so that even today his ancestral home in the lower city is preserved with great reverence.


With the influx of riches, Hytia built a tall lighthouse on Angereb, to better guide ships unfamiliar with the treacherous waters into the low island port. This in turn led to a new increase in trade vessels from distant lands, some coming from as far as the outer marches of the Sands Kingdom. Grateful for Hytia's rule and wisdom, the people of Waha Desher, led by their oracle, raised a tomb for his mentor, General Esato, which came to be known as the General's Martyr, while the fame of Kidusi Anitoni grew steadily as pilgrims came from afar, even from lands beyond the sea in the self-styled Old World, to seek its ancient wisdom. So did Taborime expand anew, and Enbesa came to an age of unrivalled wealth and splendour.
130989:
Over the centuries a new religion arose, born from the neighbouring Sands Kingdom. Reluctant to convert to the rapidly-spreading new belief, and hoping to preserve their ancestral faith, Enbesan authorities decreed all trade with the Sands Kingdom be forbidden — a bold decision which considerably imperiled Enbesa's naval and trade hegemony. This ambiguous decision — the blame for which was largely laid at the feet of Almaïr of the line of Hytia, whom historians describe as weak-willed and incompetent — led to strife among the Princes for the first time in centuries.


Believing he was the only one capable of restoring Enbesa's prosperity, Prince Yekuno of Taborime convened a great Court of Princes, during which he had all of the Princes slain, claiming the throne of Enbesa for himself. Much to his dismay, however, Almaïr survived the attempt and fled Taborime in the dark of the night with the Covenant — perhaps forewarned by a faithful servant — and was never seen again. So did the Covenant disappear from the memories of men, and its place of burial was lost.

Yekuno's rule was short-lived, however, as the kin of those he had murdered united against him in rebellion, until he eventually fell in battle after a long civil war, which left Enbesa disunited and ruined. Taborime was laid to waste, its walls torn down, and each province claimed its independence amid the chaos.

So did the Silver Age of Enbesa come to an end.
130990:
Chapter III – The Bronze Age
A Warsong of Blades



With the dissolution of Enbesa as a united nation, Angereb was swift to proclaim its independence, its princes resorting to piracy and plunder on nearby trade routes to compensate for the dearth of resources on their island. Waha Desher held their loyalty to the line of the murdered prince through the rule of his grand-daughter — a loyalty which held true through the centuries to the current day, under Emperor Ketema, and which supports their claim as the longest ruling line of modern Enbesa. Taborime, for its part, was left derelict and abandoned, a ruined testament to a lost age of prosperity spent passing between the hands of numerous minor houses and warring lords, few of them holding the city for more than a decade.


There came a time, however, when Yetbarok of the line of Almaïr ruled in one of the provinces, claiming to be of the ancient Elamais bloodline, and descended from Selamawi himself. Wielding a mighty spear reputedly wrought from one of the beams supporting the legendary Ark, he rallied many lords and armies under his charismatic rule, conquering Taborime and humbling many powerful lords under his rule. With the support of Waha Desher freely given, and the conquest of Angereb through cunning and great feats of arms, Yetbarok raised a powerful fortress on the island of Angereb and declared his rule over Enbesa, to which the people responded with great joy, for he was much-loved and admired. So began the Age of the Elamais Dynasty.
130991:
Fearing the ever-growing threat of the Sands Kingdom and the conquering ambitions of the Kashtan kings, Yetbarok raised new taxes to fund an extensive plan to construct defences in every Enbesan province. Great walls were raised around Taborime's rebuilt palace, and mighty fortifications were carved out of the living rock around Kidusi Anitoni, to ensure the temple would never again be laid waste by fire. Earth-and-stone walls sprung up all around the ksar at Waha Desher, and proud towers rose to guard the outskirts and heart of Angereb's harbour. So did Yetbarok earn the loyalty of his people as a protector of the realm.


Enbesa grew increasingly isolated and threatened as kingdoms all around its borders rallied to the young faith of the Sands Kingdom one by one. At last, a coalition, led by the Sands Kingdom, rose to quell the irreductible Enbesans once and for all, and war was waged on the outer bastions of Angereb, laying waste to the lighthouse and sinking a great many proud ships. In great haste, King Yetbarok sent most of his troops to Angereb, only to find that the Kashtan army had swept into Waha Desher on his distant flank, securing it without much resistance from the unarmed population.
130992:
Angereb stood on the brink of defeat, hope lost after Yetbarok had been slain amidst the sinking of his fleet in a disastrous battle, when unexpected allies came to change the tide of war: a powerful fleet of warships hailing from the Old World, bearing the flag of La Corona, descended upon the rear of the Sands Kingdoms' navy, sending most of their forces below the waves in a tide of fire and steel. This mighty force, mustered in great haste, had been sent to defend the last bastion of the One Faith on the continent against the encroaching Sands Kingdoms' faith. To protect the sacred lands of Enbesa, and especially Kidusi Anitoni, they crushed the invaders in a series of skillful maneuvers, until all foes had been dispersed and Enbesa was safe. In gratitude for this miraculous assistance, Yetbarok's son, Sousneyos, granted them indefinite leave to stay in his realm, and a Coronian colony soon arose in the ruins of Taborime, blossoming around a new church, as a declaration of the undying nature of the One Faith.


La Corona's influence slowly spread over Enbesa across the next century. Rebuilding much of Taborime to their standards, they established camps near Waha Desher with the hidden intent to seize Kashtan lands from this forward base with the blessing of Sousneyos and his successors. It was not until the rule of Lebne, of the Elamais Line, who ascended to the throne at a young age, that the ambitions and growing power of La Corona came to be seen as a threat.
130993:
In the last years of his father's rule, Lebne gathered support in secret from Enbesan nobles and commoners alike. His father, Zerales the Wise, saw this popularity and chose to abdicate in his son's favour, sensing a change in tides and the encroaching of old age. Without waiting for La Corona to grow accustomed to this change in power, Lebne decreed the colonizing forces to be outlaws and mustered his armies to drive them out. After a short but bloody campaign, the commanders of La Corona's colony agreed to relent and depart, outnumbered and faced with bitter resistance from the local population.

To prevent their vengeful return, Lebne ordered a vast fortress be built in Angereb, to secure the lasting safety of Angereb's outmost frontier. Basking in the popularity of his victory and youth, Lebne was granted the title of "Lebne the Great" by the people of Angereb, who proclaimed the glory of the line of the Elamais above all others.


After decades of prosperous rule, Lebne chose his grandson Mekdem to inherit the reins of Enbesa. Mekdem's brother Tomasi, however, was ambitious and cruel, and refused this decision. After Lebne's passing, he staged an attempt on Mekdem's life with the help of dissenters and ambitious nobles, assailing him and his family in the night. The coup failed, however, and both brothers were slain in the ensuing combat, while the Spear that had been deemed a token of the Elamais' legitimacy was lost in the confusion. Legend holds that an heir of Mekdem survived, but no evidence of this was ever found, and scholars believe the events of the Night of Kinstrife marked the cruel end of the Elamais Dynasty.
130994:
Chapter IV – The Iron Age
A Colossus With Iron Feet



In the years following the death of Lebne, most of Enbesa descended into unrest and chaos. Loyalists of Lebne's line took Angereb into custody and, renewed with piracy, claimed to await the return of their beloved ruler's heirs. But in the shadows of Angereb's lofty fortress, a young brigand by the name of Wag dreamt of an Enbesa united once again under a single, conquering king. From the hidden mews of Angereb to the dark corridors of Taborime's ruined palace, and the shade of the oases of Waha Desher, he gathered support. With every victory and every subtle maneuver, his fame grew, with some speaking of him as the lost son of Mekdem, of the blood of Selamawi, claiming his extraordinary military prowess as evidence.


Wag - or King Wag, as he came to be known after claiming the crowns of three of the Princes - ruled through an uneasy combination of mercy and cruelty. Those who opposed his rise to power he made brutal examples of, so that all would know to bow before him, but innocents he attempted to shield, going as far as taking the son of one of his mightiest opponents, young Ketema, as his ward, and raising him in the newly rebuilt palace of Yetbarok, at the heart of his Enbesan realm.
130995:
In time, there came an uneasy peace over King Wag's Enbesa, built upon blood shed and battles won. At this time, an expedition ordained by the pious king of the Old World's Empire came to Enbesan shores, seeking the fabled Holy Land of Kidusi Anitoni. Seeing an opportunity to expand his store of Old World technology and consolidate his rule over Enbesa, King Wag granted the expedition leave to set up a camp of soldiers and geographers in the hinterlands. Amid the confusion of their arrival, however, Ketema — by then a young ambitious man — fled Angereb to reclaim his ancestral home. Mellowed, perhaps, by the prospects promised by the expedition, King Wag chose to forgive this act of treason, much to the surprise of his councillors.


Bolstered by King Wag's welcome, the Empire sent further regiments to Enbesa, setting up a powerful camp in Waha Desher to prepare for an attack on Kashtan's unbelievers. This, however, was ill-planned, for King Wag was outraged that such a campaign had been envisioned without asking for his permission or support, and feared it would pave the way for similar conquering ambitions towards Enbesa. In his fury, the King demanded the expedition leave Enbesa under pain of war; unable to face both Kashtan hostility and possible combat with Enbesan troops, the Emperor had no choice but to relent and call for a bitter retreat to the Old World.
130996:
King Wag's hostility towards the Old World expedition was poorly judged by his people, for many had looked with hope to the foreigners for technological improvements in their daily lives. This was the starting point of King Wag's downfall. Settling ever further into sour and dangerous moods, he took Old World civilian settlers hostage to bargain for weapons and firepower — a dramatic decision which led the Empire to send a fully-armed punitive expedition his way, which tore through Enbesa, supported by vastly superior armament and discipline. Faced with his impending capture and execution, King Wag chose instead to take his own life, leaving Enbesa to be torn apart once again by the vying ambitions of warmongering princes.


As recompense for aiding them in the defeat King Wag, Empire forces granted one of the Princes, Kassa Mercha of Angereb, a vast store of advanced rifles and ammunition. Armed with this superior equipment, Kassa Mercha seized the throne as soon as the expedition had departed, crushing any dissenters with his unrivalled force.

Before he could be crowned, however, Kashtan forces crossed the border into Waha Desher, forcing Kassa Mercha to rush to face them in battle. Although the more advanced weapons and artillery inflicted heavy losses upon the invading forces, Kassa Mercha's demise in the third day of battle left the Enbesan army routed and defeated. Unable to hold Waha Desher due to their weakened numbers, the Kashtans then decided to raze the oasis to the ground, salting and burning it to ensure it would never prosper again. And so Enbesa, kingless once again, fell into greater chaos than ever before.
130997:
Amid the chaos, one man rose to power. Ketema — no longer a young, inexperienced man — raised a large, well-trained army, and took province after province under his authority, raining wrath, fire and blood upon those who had betrayed his family to King Wag's ambitions. Although victorious, this whirlwind of violence left many of the conquered populations ill-disposed towards their new sovereign, resenting him for his relentless execution of even the mildest dissenters.


Wise to the dangers of a restless population, the newly crowned King Ketema expended considerable efforts into grand and ambitious projects for his new realm, sparing no efforts to rebuild the historical capital of Taborime around a newly raised palace of splendid proportions. Claiming the title of Emperor of all Enbesa, Ketema sent envoys to Kidusi Anitoni, Waha Desher and Angereb, the last islets of independence in the realm, to negotiate terms for reconciliation and peaceful integration into the Empire. But the shadows of history, and the threat of the Old World, are never truly quelled, and there are those among the wise who fear that with the recent opening of the Grand Canal, the eyes of the allies and foes of old may turn to Enbesa, and its shores may be trod by foreign feet once more.

131323:
Governors of Kidusi


As the Seven rose, a prince was assigned to govern Kidusi Anitoni and to report matters to the Court of Taborime every year in times of prosperity. However, the priests refused to recognise the prince. Priestess Abeba the Flower relayed the reasons why to the princes in Taborime as follows:

'After the terrible attacks by the Kashta on the granary and the definitive loss of the Deathless Graces, the mighty plants imported from Sile'Amidos, we lost our purpose, our pride, and our function. But Ezana the Pacifist, King of Enbesa, refused to defend Kidusi Anitoni, nor to send any punitive expedition to the land of the thieves.

When Sûrya the Sun-King rose, and desperately looked for the Deathless Graces in Kidusi Anitoni, killing our priests and burning our library, the other islands did not intervene, and our library was destroyed.

We have no trust left in kings or princes. Kidusi Anitoni humbly requests that we be free to govern according to our own tenets and beliefs. We will continue trading for what is needed so that we may uphold our sacred scriptorial mission, and that all may know forever of Sûrya's treachery, and of the glory of the Seven.'

The princes agreed to those terms — and to ensure no tyrant ever returned to Enbesa, they decided to fund a new library on Kidusi Anitoni, to ensure the lessons of the past were never forgotten.

131327:
On the Old World


Travellers from the Old World often seek out our holy mountains, believing that they've found the mythical Land of God, Sile'Amidos. We see no reason to contradict them, as there is great power in these dreams and tales. Who will dare assault our land when powerful knights from distant lands come with vast retinues to honour our altars?

Though there is no such bounty of flowers and trees here as is described in the scripture, our knowledge of the ancient script was enough to maintain the illusion. We showed them ancient sacred texts, and bestowed upon them garbled translations to take home as divine commandments.

The holy scriptures we shared were pale copies of the content of the Ark. Written in Sile'Amidos by King Davan, who was said to have received them from the Lord himself, the Tablets of Law were purportedly hidden within the Ark, and brought through cataclysm to Enbesa by Queen Shaba. The Ark was lost in the Fall of the Seven, and many nations now claim to hold the original, without proof. But the Old World knows that the truth resides in Kidusi, as it always has since the Time of the Blessed Land.

And so, as long as the secret of the ancient script lies with Kidusi, the truth will be ours to shape. Let history judge us if it must, or let the truth be forgotten when the last of our order perish.
131328:
Symbols of Enbesa


Sile'Amidos, the heart of the world, was a land blessed by God, and a land of plenty: frankincense, myrrh, ebony, hibiscus and even the dragon tree. When it sank, the world of old was lost. History became legend, and all forgot that it is in Enbesa that the remainder of the blood of Sile'Amidos dwells. But to those who know where to look, the symbols of Sile'Amidos still pervade the land and its foundations.

The Phoenix
The dragon tree was known to shed red blood when exposed to great heat. This blood has been known since ancient times to have mystical healing properties, and legend came to claim that these qualities were endowed by the hidden roosting phoenix that nestled within its branches, the blood of which seeped into the tree with every regeneration. To this day, the people of Waha Desher still worship the Djat, one of many incarnations of the phoenix.

The Hibiscus
Long known as Deathless Grace, the hibiscus has always been associated with fertility and birth due to its red flowers, and how it blooms when it gets enough water. As such, it features in most myths as a giver of immortality. Some, including the Sun-King Sûrya, were convinced of the truth of these legends and sought the secret of the hibiscus for many years — a fruitless endeavour, and one which consumed their entire life.

The Lion
The Lion, symbol of King Selamawi of Sile'Amidos, was chosen by Queen Shaba as the protector of her new realm when the lost island sank beneath the waves. The scripture quotes her saying: 'The King is dead, but his cubs will roar his legacy over all of this Land of Lions.'

131429:
GRAMMAR
The ancient script was a figurative script rather than alphabetical: the meaning ascribed to a sign was represented by the pictogram used to manifest the concept. Most words were, however, written in combinatory fashion, so most words are compounds of several signs, each semantically significant in its own right.

SEMAGRAMS
The end-sign of each word is called a 'semagram'. Its purpose is to indicate the grammatical nature of the word to which it is attached. Examples on the Oathstone of Waha Desher are as follows:

object
adjective
person, group of persons, name, place
, , verbs (to speak, to make, to walk)

Examples:

goods
to navigate

131433:
NUMERALS

Singular nouns follow the aforementioned basic structure, whereas plurals are indicated by the sign . This sign is always found just before the determinative.

Examples:

plant
plants

CONJUCTION

Specific signs indicate a conjunctive nature between words, often a relative property:

of (indicates possession)
to, toward, for (indicates a direction)
and, with
by
131434:
TENSE

The most common tense is the present, but use of past tense has also been noted, manifested by prefixing the verb with:

Examples:

says
said

PROPER NOUNS

Proper nouns are generally exempt from grammatical modification, focusing on the core symbol behind their meaning. They are systematically suffixed with for persons and with for regions.

Examples:

Taharqa "Who-cuts-through"
Shaba "Rich-in-Plants"

THE SILVER AGE
Notes to Ketema's Steward


Enbesa's Silver Age canonically starts with the fall of King Sûrya, and the rise to power of the Seven. It is usually seen to end with the sundering of the Seven.

Questions that need answering:

- Which island was never governed by one of the Seven?
One of the islands at the time was described as 'leaderless'. The remains of the Seven's houses can be found on the islands near Taborime, where they ruled. If you can find the remaining leaders' houses, we'll be able to deduct the leaderless island. Look for isolated or prominent houses.

-How large was Taborime?
By all accounts, the city flourished under the Seven's rule. Finding the ancient city walls could help estimate the limits of the city at the time. It can't have been much greater than the city today, so perhaps look near the city's current borders?

Note: Please report back as soon as possible.

132312:
THE BRONZE AGE
Notes to Ketema's Steward


Scholars attest that Enbesa's Bronze Age began with the unification of the land under the rule of Yetbarok, heir of Selamawi, after the fall of the Seven, and ended when Lebne's grandson was murdered in Angereb, barely a century ago.

Despite this recent history, some questions remain unanswered:

- The roster of works built by Yetbarok is incomplete.
He is known for his many defensive installations against the Sands Kingdoms in Angereb, Taborime and Kidusi, as well as the ksar walls on Waha Desher. Investigate each of these and report to me.

- Where is the fabled hidden access to the Temple on Kidusi Anitoni?
Yetbarok was known for building secret passages in his strongholds, for fear of successful invasions. While the passage on Angereb and the mountain pass on Waha Desher are known, the passage below the temple on Kidusi remains hidden. Perhaps you could find it?

Note: Please report back as soon as possible.

Tourists are a special resident type who stay in Hotels in your city, and have various basic and luxury needs. Rather than provide workforce like other residents, Tourists are customers who visit Restaurants, Cafés, Bars and other Tourist Hotspots in your city.

Tourist customers are represented by the suitcase icon.
134607: Your existing Public Mooring will have to be upgraded to a Tourist Mooring before Tourists can visit your island. Click the upgrade button inside the Public Mooring building to upgrade.
134609:
Hotels do not count as residences, and therefore cannot be upgraded.

To keep Hotels full, you should strive to keep your Tourists happy. You can do this by improving your city's attractiveness, fulfilling luxury needs, and connecting them to Tourist Hotspots by bus. Tourist Hotspots are cultural attractions like the Zoo and the Museum.

Taller or equal height skyscrapers are colored in brown.

Click on the "?" in the skyscraper menu to get more information on the Panorama Effect.

137677:
Both Engineer and Investor residences can be upgraded to skyscrapers.
This is only possible once they have full population, and all basic needs have been fulfilled.
Engineer skyscrapers can have up to three levels, while investor skyscrapers can have up to five levels. Each level brings with it new needs for their residents.

Skyscrapers have significant maintenance costs. Manage your income and expenditure accordingly!
137679:
Select any Engineer or Investor residence and click on the button to add a skyscraper level. This will require elevators, which can be produced in the assembly line.

You can also remove skyscraper levels, eventually turning the skyscraper back into a regular residence.

Once built, you can change the appearance of each level by clicking the brush icon.

Tip: Hold while having a skyscraper selected to see all skyscrapers at the same level.
137681:
Skyscraper residents like to have an unobstructed, panoramic view when looking out of their windows. With this in mind, you can create Panorama Effects on skyscrapers.

The Panorama Effect of a skyscraper increases the population that can live in it, and reduces its maintenance cost.
137683:
There are, in total, five different strengths of Panorama Effect, all of which increase the population of a particular skyscraper.
The effect grows in strength based on the number of smaller skyscrapers around it.
137684: Note that you will not be punished for maintaining no Panorama Effect: the skyscraper will still have the regular population amount.
137687:
Each individual skyscraper counts other skyscrapers within a certain radius when calculating its Panorama Effect. The higher that skyscraper is, the bigger its radius will be.
Regular residences are not taken into account!

The sum of all modifiers determines the Panorama Effect that the selected skyscraper will get.
This will never go below zero, or above five.

All Skyscrapers within the green street overlay range of the Shopping Arcade have their need for it fulfilled.

For Skyscraper residents, any active design patent will fulfill their need for the respective Shopping Arcade.
Depending on the chosen design patent, there are a variety of beneficial effects on residences within a radius of the Shopping Arcade.
137724:
Recipe books allow you to pick a single active product for Shopping Arcades from a selection. Multifactories such as Orchards or Assembly Lines have catalogues that follow the same principle.

They are accessed from the respective building's menu.
137726:
Behold the modern Skyline Tower — the final building introduced with The High Life. As with all Monuments there are several phases to its construction, and only one Skyline Tower can be built per island.

The Skyline Tower also has significant maintenance costs. Manage your income and expenditure accordingly!
137728:
The Skyline Tower is, in principle a residence just like other skyscrapers. Thus, an exorbitantly high number of investors can live in it.

Skyline Tower residents simply cannot do enough shopping: the wider variety of shopping arcade products there are available, anywhere on the island, the more the tower’s population will increase.

Take note though, that the Investors acquired from shopping arcades do not consume any other goods, so are essentially "free".

Dear Isabel,

Thanks to you, the Pyrphorians have been driven from our region; but their legacy remains.
139954: The generator they left behind — the generator we were forced to build during their loathsome occupation — is polluting our land.
139955: My people depend on the electricity the generator provides, but it is killing our island: our rivers are choked with filth; the smog-filled air drives the birds from the trees; even the soil suffers a slow poisoning.
139956: But we have a plan: a hydroelectric dam! My people have the knowledge and the skill, but we need your leadership to build a new, sustainable town for the workers, and help us complete the dam.
139958: And that tree, which had stood on the island for centuries, is the tree that is represented by the logo of the Eden Initiative today.
139959: Do we truly expect to be able to create an Eden, a perfect world? Perhaps not.
139960: No solutions are ever perfect – certainly the hydroelectric dam built by Isabel Sarmento and Yaosca Rodriguez wasn’t. It disrupted fish migration, caused unintended damage to the ecosystem, increased the risk of floods.
139961: But if we must choose between imperfection and inaction, there can only be one answer. We can always improve our designs and implement mitigations – what we cannot do is sit idly by while our world collapses.
139962: What Isabel and Yaosca did represented a bold step forward. With the knowledge and technology we possess today, we can do so much more — and it would be inexcusable not to try.

800350: A nervous sailor rows towards the line of mines. The makeshift grappling hooks trailing behind his dinghy are intended to drag mines out of the path of the expedition ship. 800351: The idea is a terrible one from the start. The lengthy poles, comprised of other poles, are unwieldy and inaccurate, even in the hands of a several strong men. Few are left to bail water, when so many lie dead or injured.
800352: Go through diplomatic papers in search of any clues
800353: The search is a fruitful one. The well-organised diplomatic library includes a comprehensive folio of papers on nearby mine positions. You stop by the outpost and pick up anything that looks useful.
800354: The search is worthwhile. After a few hours scouring the diplomatic archives, a paper on nearby mine positions is found. This gives the navigators the difficult task of charting a safe course through the waters. No-one is quite sure if the information given is up-to-the-minute, but when the last line of mines is cleared, all are suitably relieved.
800355: The documents in the ship archives at first seem exact. A map is discovered showing the mine positions. The reckless blunder has cost no lives, but the significant task of repair greatly wearies the crew.
800356: Optimism makes way for abject terror, as the map of mines that is found and used for navigation turns out to be completely false. 800360: Tell them to stay on the ship

800363: For the godless dinghy, doom seems inevitable the moment it drops and a man slops overboard. This inauspicious beginning foreshadows the disaster to follow. 800364: It is horrifying that most significant members of the crew are aboard this fragile dinghy. The crew are understandably devastated at the destruction they have witnessed first-hand. Life feels as if it may never be the same again.
800365: Your faith goes untried in the nervous silence, as the ship escapes the mine trap the same way it entered. All agree they should never have ended up in a minefield in the first place.
800366: Your faith does not go untried. The sinister cones have moved about over time, and no matter how truly the ship follows its original course, it is inevitable a mine will burst into the hull. 800367: None of it is of any use. Your godforsaken crew do not realise how the sinister cones move about over time. No matter how true the course, more than one mine shakes the ship's belly as it limps clear. Many lives are lost, and the damage to the ship is severe.
800396: You found a tourist that offers to trade with you.
800441: You have found a radiant relic! The crew toast the success of your archaeological expedition. May we now better understand what it is to be human!
800448: You have captured a wild animal! The crew toast the success of your zoological expedition. This can only aid studies of the natural world!
800454: You have earned a reward for your altruism! The crew toast a successful rescue, with all returning to the glad comforts of home.
800460: You have discovered pirate bounty! With the dread buccaneers blown out of the water, a search of their sunken wreck unearths a well-deserved reward!
800468: A matter of the heart. The crew have been enjoying some island hospitality, but many are now refusing to leave. They have fallen in love with the sons and daughters of the local king. 800471: Convince the king your crew's affection is genuine
800472: Await the verdict of the copper oracle
800473: Leave without the crew who've fallen in love

800475: The king is delighted to see his children wed. Delicate understanding of local custom and a smattering of their language allow a message of true love to be conveyed. For his departing children, it shall be the longest, most fascinating honeymoon.
800476: Something is lost in translation. Yet the king smiles benignly, as if your crew still have a chance to prove themselves. 'He suggests a great hunt,' says your diplomat, 'or else we may await arcane judgment.' His eyes flick to a copper oracle on a dais.
800477: The awkward gestures and diagrams in the sand prove highly offensive to the king and his people. Sensing outrage, the crew back away towards the ship. The angry locals fire arrows at their former amours. Fittingly, one is struck in the heart, and bleeds out into the brine. The rest return lovelorn, to their dreary maps and compasses.
800478: Capture the king a prize animal
800479: Face the verdict of the copper oracle
800480: The hunt goes quite well. Beautiful boars inhabit the woods, and though tricky to catch, are little trouble for your experts. Though the king will still not allow you to leave with his children, the feast of boar brings everyone together in the moment. The lovers understand this moment is all they have, and the next morning there is an acceptance that it is time to part ways.
800481: The hunt is not perfect. The crew show courage in pursuit of a tiger, which draws the king's admiration. Sadly, they cannot catch it, which leaves the king wondering if your men will be able to provide once married. Thus, he decides not to let his children leave. Some of your crew remain committed to staying behind, and it is with regret you must continue without them.
800482: Your naive hunters fail the test. Forest deer are everywhere, and hunting them hardly seems a challenge. Had your so-named 'hunters' any respect for nature, they'd have realised the sacred deer were not what the king was after. Instead they gather them up greedily. The king makes it perfectly clear your expedition must move on. With heavy hearts, the sailors return to the ship.
800483: The oracle predicts a reassuring fate for all. Those who wish to remain for love will live fulfilling lives, but the same shall be true for those still committed to your expedition. All parties feel a sense of peace. Your voyage shall continue without any resentment towards those it leaves behind.
800484: The copper oracle is disappointingly undecided. The king cannot, in good faith, allow his children to leave to an uncertain destiny. His ultimatum is that your crew become part of his extensive family or else they must leave alone. Though understandable, it is nevertheless regrettable when some decide to stay behind.
800485: The copper oracle predicts that your souls cannot be saved. With your crew rotten to the core, the king makes it clear there can be no union with his children, and that you are no longer welcome. Heart-broken and bearing the burden of sin, the crew return to the triviality of duty.
800486: The copper oracle sees only purity in your crew's hearts. It predicts a bounteous future for the king's children, and so with tearful pride, he gives the couples his blessing. The traditional ceremony is both spiritually uplifting and wholesome.
800487: The copper oracle reveals a little doubt in your crew's hearts. The king interprets that his children will only be happy if they remain on the island., and that some of your sailors are not in love, but merely infatuated. Still, you must lose the fine crew who have formed genuine bonds.
800488: The copper oracle reveals great doubt in your crew's hearts. The king does not for a minute believe that your inconstant crew are as deep in love as they claim. If they cannot demonstrate otherwise, it might be better if your people left.
800489: The copper oracle proclaims your crew's hearts sinful and wicked. Arm-in-arm with their new-found amours, the sailors await some happy answer. But the moment the king's arm is raised, daggers unsheathe, plunging into the hearts of the would-be lovers. Speechless and unharmed, the rest are free to leave the island, pondering the grave cost of faithlessness.
800490: Try to convince the king your crew are worthy
800491: Order the crew to leave at once
800492: Careful diplomacy has him thinking twice. Perhaps there is a way for the crew to prove themselves. A lean champion steps forward. Fighting him may impress the king, or else you can try and outhunt him.
800493: The king is offended by your insolence. Without a word he boards a boat and heads out to sea. Some foolishly follow, believing he can be reasoned with, but they have even less knowledge of local boats than local customs. Their bodies will be dredged from the reef as your tactless expedition struggles on.
800496: You have your champions. One-by-one the suitors fight the king's champion. Those who prevail, it turns out, are permitted to take their lovers to sea. Some fail, but can at least drown their sorrows during the farewell celebration that follows.
800497: It is not a pleasant sight for the faint of heart. Your best champion is put forward, and subsequently knocked about the head for the entirety of the contest. At the end a cloth is needed to conceal the disfigured face. The king expresses his condolences for your loss, but all is fair in love and war.
800498: It is close but the king's champion is outfoxed. By sundown your best hunter has claimed six boars to their five. The king will still not allow you to leave with his children, but the feast of boar brings everyone together in one moment. The lovers understand a moment is all they have, and the next morning there is an acceptance that it is time to part ways.
800499: Lacking the skill, your hunters try to cheat. Without knowledge of the island's fauna, they decide to follow the king's hunters in the hope of poaching the animal they are tracking. But they are led a merry dance. Three days pass, and your champion is missing presumed dead. The crew have no choice but to depart, tail between their legs.
800500: Paradise lost! The expedition may be back underway, but the mood is abject as the beautiful island becomes but painful memory. Too painful for one, who is discovered dead, it is said, by way of a broken heart.
800501: It is a significant blow. Any happiness the crew might feel at their comrades finding love is consumed by feelings of resentment. How could they have been so selfish? The expedition goes on, but those who are still a part must take on twice as much work.

800504: The Midshipman is found with his throat slit, knife in hand. It would appear to be suicide, but appearances often prove deceptive. Understandably, the whole crew crowd the scene, debating whether he was the type to take his own life, or if someone might have gained by his passing. Needless to say, they expect some action be taken...
800506: The Expert will have the answers
800508: Do nothing, it's suicide - nothing more to be said
800509: There are gasps of macabre delight, as the famous detective reveals the only possible solution. 'Elementary you see. Look at this tiny moth wing on the body. The detective lunges across the deck and secures the watchman, who being as impressed with the deduction as everyone else, readily admits to having sought to gain rank by the murder.
800510: Careful analysis of the scene reveals two leads. Some believe an autopsy would leave the facts of the case plain, while others reckon the little time available should be spent analysing any evidence at the scene that might establish whodunnit.
800511: This lot aren't bloodhounds that's for sure, and turn up nothing even with a strong whiff of murder about it all. With the incompetent investigation ending conspicuously silent, the crew must last the remainder of the expedition in fear they are marked next on the list.
800512: Conduct an autopsy of the body
800513: Fashion a tool for gathering forensic evidence

A letter, found later, serves to explain that the fellow knew he hadn't long to live, and wished to face death in his own way. The crew are galvanised on hearing this story of bravery.
800515: The autopsy is sufficient to confirm it was murder. Strangulation was the cause of death, not a slit throat - which was added post-mortem. All else remains unknown. Nevertheless, with the cause of death established, the list of suspects is narrowed down to just a few who had the means and the motive for the crime.
800516: The autopsy is dreadfully clumsy, and leaves the body almost unrecognisable. The unschooled 'medic' evidently have a point to prove, and insist on defiling it further, despite being a bundle of nerves. By the end the morgue looks like a butchery, and the stricken mortician runs wildly about the ship, scalpel in hand. Several are injured trying to restrain him, but the psychological trauma of an unsolved mystery is twice as damaging.
800519: You out the grim truth. The alibi of one sailor does not match his fellows, and he cracks, confessing to the midshipman's murder. It transpires the midshipman had bragged of bedding the other man's wife. The murderer expresses only remorse for his crime, and as the noose is placed around his neck, the crew regret that justice must be so severe.
800520: The interrogation is painfully haphazard. Though it is clear one of the suspects must be the killer, lines of inquiry fail to produce answers. No option remains but to offload all the suspects at the next port to prevent further incident. It is a source of great shame to the crew that fine innocent sailors are certain to be among them.
800521: A brutal approach, but one delivering quick results. It seems the midshipman was preparing to whistle-blow unauthorised smuggling below deck, and was killed for it. The ringleaders threatened others with a similar fate if they didn't keep quiet. The culprits are unceremoniously shot, and the vulgar matter is over.
800522: Torture seldom results in happiness. Your victim screams a confession, perhaps in the hope it will end the pain. With nothing else to go on, you scapegoat the poor beggar, and he is keelhauled until dead. The crew are in no doubt that this was the wrong man, and hope to escape your inhuman expedition at the first opportunity.
800523: What innovation! A bright young spark applies some of the latest forensic researches. When the crew prints are taken, the guilty party is collared in the most satisfying modern fashion!
800524: It's complicated identifying footwear and gait. Ambitious of the crew, then, to attempt to solve both problems with the one device. 800525: Fragile justice! As your craftsmen stare at an empty drawing board, gormless sailors think they help by tidying up the crime scene. 800527: Put the fear of god into the suspects
800528: Dump all the suspects at the next port, and be done with it

800530: The trial is a farce. Sailors bark questions from the sidelines which the suspects are quite within their rights to leave unanswered. But this obstinacy serves only to rile the shouting mob! 800533: These are not god-fearing sailors, and hear the priest's weak plea for the killer to come forward with impassive expressions. Perhaps there is a different approach.

800564: Hunters find tracks, but can't say what made them. The marks are indeed strange - disturbing almost. Claw marks that go deep in the decking, as if the unspeakable thing that made them was in some frenzy.

Their livers have been removed.
800567: Build a trap to catch whatever it is

800577: Use a reflective object to signal help

800586: Ask at the fort for help
800587: Ignore the fort and continue along the path

The journey is a wearying lament for a fallen friend, meandering slowly back to civilisation.

800595: A wild goose chase to desolation. Though the ostrich your crew have found cannot fly, it lollops along at surprisingly high speed. 800596: Your reprobates have no knowledge of desert mysteries. The divining rod has wasted enough of your time, and your caravan is nearly through the water.

Your crew feel blessed, and the expedition can resume with new-found devotion.
800600: Are the gods testing you? You wait and wait but there is not yet a sign.

800609: Attack the bear blocking the way
800611: Boooooom! The valley shudders with the sweet stench of exploded dynamite. The bears hurry away, leaving the crew thoroughly entertained at the superiority of mankind and the power of invention.
800612: Trust in the expert hunters never feels misplaced, even when they recommend the party break into passionate song. For singing the shanty 'Cheerly-ay-oh' brings the crew together, whilst also dispersing the wary bears deep into the forest.
800613: The hunters lack guile. They have enough to lead the crew on a route silent as a church, but not enough to stop a bear sniffing them out. It's easy to believe from its vacant eyes, that it sees you as a potentially delicious kind of threat.
800614: Call themselves hunters! The tracks thought to lead away from bear territory go instead to a clearing at its heart. The bears at first seem alarmed their picnic is disturbed, until they realise your crew are on the menu. The sound of crunching bone rings in the ears of the few that manage to flee.
800617: The bear's face proves a good target. Ducking the terrifying whooshes of its paws, someone manages to prime their pistol and shoot it through the eye. The bear drops dead. No-one feels particularly good about killing it, but the way ahead is now clear.
800618: Adaptation is good when a fight isn't going well. The bear flinches but does not drop after the first round of gunfire. There is no time to reload, before it is upon them with its paws. Knocked down the men are smart enough to play dead. After an hour or so facing the floor, the bears lose interest and leave. The crew are able to lick their wounds, and move on.
800619: It's easy to underestimate mummy bears. As the soldiers fluff the loading of their weapons, the bear nonchalantly grasps one by the wrist, and sinks her jaw into his neck. The others panic and flee with their arms in the air. She pursues a second, striking him dead against a rock. Now she and her cubs can finally be left in peace.
800620: Sometimes it helps to know your hill contours. The crew carefully fall away, circumventing the bear's position, and keeping their backs to the mountainside. With the higher ground, the bear appears to lose interest. Hearts pumping, the crew hurry to safety.
800621: Stupidly the crew decide to run, and reach a dead-end. The bear pursues at a leisurely speed, yet with no less menace, and the crew are forced to seek refuge in a cave, or else try climbing the trees.
800623: Hide in the cave and pray
800625: Against all anxiety, the Bear doesn't follow. Still, the men in the cave are too afraid to light a fire, or sleep through the night. Shattered and hungry, they emerge the next morning, only to find their sacrifice was wholly unnecessary.
800626: Bears can see terribly well in the dark, and since your crew have stumbled into its house, where its vulnerable infants sleep, it is not very happy. The crew that do manage to break for daylight have clothes ragged and torn, and cannot speak, for it is clear they were the lucky ones.
800627: The crew climb the trees well enough, but the bear isn't going to make their lives easy. It is a full day and night before it gives up shaking trunks, or climbing halfway up towards the dangling crew. When it finally leaves, the exhausted crew descend, their nerves in shreds.
800628: Bears are awfully good at climbing trees, and as on this occasion, it is not uncommon to see them strike their adversaries from the branches. Its hapless victim plunges from the canopy and lands like a sack of red berries on rocks below. Others injure themselves as the men drop from the trees in a desperate escape.
800629: The lone bear's haunch is picked out with expert marksmanship. It staggers before bounding off into the woods. Your crew are delighted to return to the safety of the ship, whilst also having done the mighty beast no lasting harm.
800630: The first volley of shots miss, and the bear attacks. A second shot finds its mark, and the wounded bear escapes into the trees, but a man lies dead. His brother cries revenge, and is already off into the woods to hunt the grisly killer.
800631: Out here, bears rule. The wildly inaccurate gunfire serves only to rile the bear into a frenzy, and draw attention to your position. Then a second, larger bear thunders from the undergrowth and mauls a man to death. A few of your piffling soldiery manage to escape with all their limbs attached.
800632: Track the wounded bear with him
800634: Bittersweet. Your fine tracking skills allow the crew to catch up with the bear and watch it from hiding. It is a she-bear, and is now nuzzling its young cubs. 'That is why she killed him,' says the brother, gone all vitriol. 'Let us leave, and hope my brother's spirit may somehow live on in this place.'
800635: The hot-headed hunt is a success none celebrate. Once found, the bear no longer has strength to defend itself. As the brother drives a stake into its heart, it gives over with a last sad sigh. In that moment a tiny cub pads into the open, crawling weakly under the limp arm of its mother. If only they had understood, the crew could have saved the heartache.
800636: Hunting is impossible with passions running this high. When another man snaps a twig, the vengeful brother attacks him wildly, and the others fail to intervene. The brother's eyes glaze as he slides to the earth, bayonet in his back.
800637: The decision is unpopular. 'Stubborn 'til the end,' say those in the minority. But the greater part have things to say on the subject of dishonour. 'Those brothers loved each other to the end,' remarks one old sailor, 'and what little love did we show for them...'
800638: The bears have no chance. Indeed, the camouflage is so good, the crew can barely see one another! Thickly daubed in the colours of the forest, the chameleon crew bypass the bears with ease. A story of ingenuity at which their grandchildren shall marvel!
800639: Even the most hardened sailors find the smell unbearable. Not to mention the indignity of covering oneself in bear excrement for longer than is perfectly necessary. Eventually though the bears depart, leaving the reeking crew free to have a much-needed wash.
800640: Dressing as pantomime trees is a bad idea, and as the bears attack, the flimsy branches the crew intended to cover their faces prove no more effective in self-defence. The ensuing scene might have made for an impressive spectacle on the stage, though only as the most gruesome of tragedies.
800664: The crew are beset by insatiable and painful itching! From lieutenants down to pigeon-keepers, they twist and turn in their bunks and cannot sleep. It is affecting their capacity to carry out the most basic duties, something must be done!
800667: Find somewhere to stop and be rid of it
800668: Let them itch, it's common at sea
800669: Washing a splendid idea at sea? Who knew?! The itching is very soon forgotten, as the sailors cavort through rainbows of expurgating bubbles. The rich perfume below deck is a welcome reminder of family and bygone days.
800670: 'Only jellyfish!' says the cultivated doctor cheerfully. 'Our refreshing swim at that cove appears to be the cause. It must have been rife with their larvae!' The crew marvel at the clever diagnosis, and as the itching subsides, bask in the pioneering case-study they have performed for the benefit of humankind.
800671: The red welts seem to perplex the doctor. 'There is evidence of the parasitic,' he splutters as he peers through his magnifying glass, 'but then it could be nothing at all!'
800672: The doctor is a demented quack. When the condition is established correctly as crusted scabies - contagious, but hardly dangerous - the doctor's experiment is for the affected to bathe in an acid solution. Needless to say, his victims do not survive their injuries. When the expedition returns, it is entirely possible he may be stripped of his profession.
800673: Examine the cabins for some sort of parasite
800674: Have the afflicted bathe in holy water
800675: There are bedbugs everywhere! There must be something that can be done to exterminate these disc-bodied hangers-on!
800676: They cannot see the wood for the trees! Evidence of fleas would be everywhere to the right pair of eyes. Two weeks pass, and murine typhus breaks out. Rashes, fever and vomiting grip the fleas' hosts, who are never able to find the cause of their itching agony.
800679: The matter is craftily 'put-to-bed'. Despite the time-consuming upheaval, the crew are surprised to have their cabins so well refurbished. 'They're too soft on us,' says a jolly cove inspecting the new bunks, but my britches haven't itched all day.'
800680: What dreary decor!' says the Lieutenant tartly. Matters deteriorate when some ill-fashioned bunks collapse. 'I'd rather have the itching back,' says an exhausted-looking sailor. Like others, he has to sleep out on the hard decking, until some competent craftsmen can come aboard.
800681: It is a job half-done. For most the problem goes away, but some must live with the itching. Wherever the bugs' nasty little hidey-hole is, it must still reel with lousy punters, each telling stories of the sailor blood they drained the night before.
800682: The priest's most divine bottle does the trick. 'This water is indeed holy!' he says, as the fearsome muscovite vodka from 1791 is uncorked and slapped over the itches of the queuing sailors. 'Shame to use it like this, but I'd rather sleep,' he cackles.
800683: 'Is nothing sacred anymore?' Says the priest, who turns up his nose at the suggestion of using his water for something so humdrum. 'The lord hath bigger fish to fry,' he says pointedly. As well as the vile and incessant itching, the crew now have a parsimonious priest to contend with.
800684: Sand and sun is a panacea! An acute sense of direction leads the ship to an island paradise. A freshwater lagoon relieves the itching, and the much-needed relaxation will stand all in good stead for the journey ahead.
800685: Bringing contagion to port might be a bad idea. The itching is at its worst by the time the expedition reaches the bustling alien seaport, something the local authorities don't fail to notice. The harbour-master's tug escorts you to quarantine. How do you escape?
800686: It's impossible for your aimless navigators to concentrate. The expedition fidgets wildly off course, with no land in sight. Meanwhile the assassin bugs continue to spread their dreadful disease. Even they'd probably make better navigators! Then there wouldn't have to be quite so much death!
800687: Lie that the sickness isn't contagious
800688: Threaten them into letting you go
800690: The lie works like a charm. A doctor promptly comes aboard to confirm this hypothesis. Although she sternly points out the condition is contagious after all, she also recognises it to be a mild complaint. 'Crabs,' the translator says, face flushing. The crew are too relieved to feel embarrassed.
800692: It is obvious you are lying, and the authorities are not impressed. They allow several days to pass, without any word on your ship's release, adversely affecting the morale of your crew.
800693: They don't want any trouble. A doctor comes aboard ship and goes nervously about his business. Although the atmosphere is somewhat cagey, medicines for your crew's skin conditions are provided, and the expedition can continue on its way.
800694: You underestimate them. Two surprise warships hove round the landspit and close in to firing range. There is no choice but to run. As your ship crashes wildly out between jetties, the escort ship pincers, and opens fire. The effect is catastrophic. Your modest vessel flees in tatters, and many good sailors are dead or wounded. For the rest, the itching is set to continue.
800695: It's a long time before the authorities deal with you, with bureaucracy seemingly a way of life here. When you finally have access to a medical professional, there is already a post-mortem to be conducted. It appears chemicals leeched into the water supply and caused the rashes and sickness. With the water changed, the others recover, but it cannot redeem the loss of a life.
800696: It is a particularly awful itch however. The disgusting lice infesting the ship, and discomfort thereof has many questioning the worth of your expedition. There is only so much scratching a crew can take before they lose all appetite for the journey ahead.
800698: Widespread suspicion is the undesirable outcome. Ignorance of the full circumstances surrounding the death has the crew feeling powerless. You must accept that quarrels and accusations will now be routine until the end of this expedition.
800877: These parasites must have come from the marsh goo; all that waist-high wading. Now they nestle deep in your crew, who, at risk of harm from their own madcap cures, really need professional help!
800881: A delectable disinfectant! The suffering take immense pleasure scouring themselves in a whacking great tub of the stuff. Indeed, so diverting is this new form of alcohol absorption, that even those without parasites take turns.
800882: The doctor concocts a panacea, which not only purges the belly-dwelling roundworm, but more besides. Garlic, wormwood, and lemon quietly see off a myriad other complaints of your spoon-dodging sailors.
800883: The doctors disagree. 'Madam! Bloodletting gives our patients only a fifty-fifty chance!' says one. 'Sir, tinctures are seldom beneficial OR effective on parasites!' says the other.
800884: It does go away, eventually. 'My arm looked like a wormcake for a while,' one sailor laments, 'but that little smattering of holes filled-up with pus now - signs my body is winning the war.'
800885: Mass amputation for all?! The festering parasites have gnawed their way to bone! Limbs must be chopped, or else their bodies shall rattle with bemaggoted cavities!
800889: A fine placebo. As if by magic, the intestinal worms lose the will to go on. The doctor freely admits this is more likely down to positive patient attitude, than his revolting tincture.
800890: The unpleasant medicine doesn't help. Constant trips to the privy are now the only release for your bug-ridden crew. The doctor admits to the failure of the tincture, but thankfully has something for diarrhoea.
800891: The tincture is poison! Having seen their first shipmate choke on his dose, the rest decide they'd rather live with a six-foot tapeworm in their bellies.
800892: Somehow it works, and the patients are rid of the parasite. The doctor seems unsurprised, 'human physiology may be complex, but treatment need not be.' A pretty vague case summary, but who cares?!
800893: Perfect preparation for amputation! At least that's what your crazed doctor would have you believe. Once her macabre experiment is concluded there is surely only one course of action for the afflicted...the crew are aghast.
800894: It does go away, eventually. 'My arm looked like a wormcake for a while,' one sailor laments, 'but that little smattering of holes filled-up with pus now - signs my body is winning the war.'
800895: Mass amputation for all?! The festering parasites have gnawed their way to bone! Limbs must be chopped, or else their bodies shall rattle with bemaggoted cavities!
800901: As good as could be expected. Out with parasites, in with polished peg legs and helpful hook-hands. The crew look not nearly as enthusiastic as you might think however.
800902: Extraordinary that you trusted that quack! She is sideshow surgeon, carving up her victims with the zeal of a ripper, and the accuracy of a pissing schoolboy. At least the screams will die away soon enough...
800903: Nothing can save them. Though a mercy that they may choose their manner of death - unmolested by the ship's quack - it is death nonetheless. The parasite has sucked the life from your expedition.
800933: Trapped in the snow! When the furious blizzard relents, the exploration party see the mountain pass ahead is blocked. Some say the rough terrain can be crossed, others say they saw a small fork in the path not too far back.
800935: Craft something to traverse the terrain
800938: The crew feel happy awe, at the resulting avalanche. There, as the pass beyond is revealed, they swear they see something lurching away. Giant and hirsute, it leaves no print but in the imagination.
800939: The skis are highly effective. Simply fashioned, and with a clever coating of paraffin. Some prove expert skiers, glissading with a flourish to the finish line, but all make it to the bottom. The whole thing has turned out to be a good bit of fun.
800943: It is not much of a detour. The going is steady and before long the warm fire of the base camp appears in view. The blizzard is something to tell the grandchildren, provided frostbite hasn't seen to that...
800944: The path is both steep and perilous. A narrow ledge along a sheer cliff lies ahead. Some men are ready to give up. All the while a strange noise keens below the gnashing gale.
800945: A far more treacherous path, but your crew are committed now. A steep cliff ahead must be negotiated, and your ropes are too short.
800946: Shelter is minimal. Huddling cannot keep out the cold. When a rescue party arrives with equipment the next morning, they find men frostbitten and hypothermic. Not all of them will survive the journey down.
800947: Toboggans are better where it's flat. Though solidly made, the going is fast. One sled veers into a ravine. A cry below: 'Officer injured', but the wind is picking up.
800948: The clumsy snowshoes fail you. Whether it is in their design or construction, every step sinks the party deeper. The cold will claim lives before the storm is weathered.
800952: The doctor works quickly. Just what is needed with another blizzard brewing. 'Temporary strapping,' he says, 'but should get us home.' The officer and rest of the party make shelter with little time left to spare.
800953: The doctor knows nothing of urgency. 'Give my patient space!' he snaps at those trying to move things along. Meanwhile, a blizzard sweeps the ravine, and the onset of frostbite is enough to split the party. Neither the doctor nor his unfortunate patient are to be seen again.
800954: You knew deep down not all would make it. 'They're all returned but the injured fellow,' comes the news. 'There was no saving him, the way he was. Ice stripped the meat from his bones like a chef's mandorre.'
800956: Urge your party to face their fears
800957: A heavenly, enlightened voice calls. None stop to look down, so enchanted are they. Over a verge, appears a shrine with a great bell - the source of the sound - and beyond, a pilgrims' path to the foot of the mountain.
800958: A non-believer falls to his death. 'Those lacking conviction shall be tried and judged in this place,' echoes the priest. The rest edge to safety, consoled by the apparent goodness in their hearts.
800960: Nothing but a demonic howl. The blizzard rises anew. Without hope to keep them aloft, it is no surprise when a ledge gives way, damning to hell below.
800961: A song of solidarity rises through the line of snow-crusted faces. Clinging to what they most cherish, they edge to safety. Had they not been reminded of such incentives, it is doubtful they would have survived.
800962: Only some take strength. The rest remain in a frozen huddle. They may have lacked courage to negotiate the high ledge, but will welcome in their icy death with creditable stoicism.
800965: Craft longer ropes and swing down
800966: All are saved, at a cost. Putting the ropes together is quite a task with frozen fingers. That the party are able to cling to the rope as they descend is a small miracle. Nevertheless, frostbite will do lasting damage to their digits.
800967: A small but critical detail is overlooked. Grip. A man falls from the top of the rope with a cry, tumbling those below him into the abyss like meat from a skewer. Only a few frozen grimaces survive.
800968: It is a risky business. Though the cliff isn't lacking in handholds, this is a test of individual endurance. Some were never going to be up to it. As they fall, the will to survive in the others strengthens.
800973: Everything points towards the fiery gate. It appears like a hallucination, an ancient stone doorway suffused with blue flame set into the rock face. Perhaps a long lost people constructed it, as a shortcut through the high ridge dividing the region. Your men consider it an auspicious sign, and would like to enter it, but perhaps it would be safer to take the long way through the dense jungle.
800974: Have the scientist inspect the gate
800975: Have faith and leap through the flames
800976: Wrap up in something before leaping through
800978: The scientist banishes the illusion. "The fire that you perceive around the gate is simply an agglomeration of azure glow-worms." Laughter becomes delight, as the party take the pulsing creatures in hand. Indeed, they are of great help in navigating the dark tunnel to the far side of the ridge, saving you days of trekking.
800979: If anything the flames are cool, like bundles of ribbons brushing the skin. This gate is, without question, an earthly manifestation of the divine, for not far along the tunnel, the light breaks in once more, and your party arrive on the far side of the ridge, spiritually tranquil, and having saved days of trekking.
800980: Some of the crew remain doubtful. Drawing a little closer to the gate, they are surprised to feel no heat coming from the fire. One leap of faith and they would be through! Still, they hesitate, for a perfect human skeleton lies just the other side of the threshold.
800981: Alas! Fire and brimstone! Some of the crew seem entranced by the glowing entrance. The temperatures are volcanic, but the diabolic procession of fanatics are numb to the pain. The others watch horrified, as fabric, skin and flesh renders before their eyes. It makes the long way round seem a miracle of mercy.
800982: Try to determine how the person died
800984: The doctor forms a decent hypothesis, and the crew are convinced. "Even from afar, I can see the bones are in poor condition; not burned, but malnourished." Anxious not to end up the same way, the crew take a gamble, and are astonished to discover that leaping through the gate does them no harm. They follow the tunnel to the other side of the ridge. "I wonder if it was those frogs we licked..." the doctor mumbles.
800985: A little knowledge is a dangerous thing. Your doctor makes several sweeping assumptions, finally concluding, "exhaustion, I'm quite certain. That they died at this particular place is only a coincidence." As the first volunteer crosses the threshold, flames grasp his ankles, then shoot rapidly up and over his body. He drops upon the stone floor, taking his place beside the last poor fool. Horrified, your expedition must go the long way round.
800986: "Ouch!" The men yelp, rolling in the stone passageway beyond, until they are sure they are no longer aflame. With the strange gate behind them, your brave soldiers compare their ugly burns as they march through the tunnel to the far side of the ridge.
800987: "Cowards!" Your men lack the discipline to follow a simple order! You will have to find another way.
800988: They make it. Rolled-up like carpets, they skip over the strange and fiery threshold. As they wend their way through the passage to the other side of the ridge, their worst complaint is the overwhelmingly sweet pong of sweat that is sure to follow them for the rest of the journey. Still, all remain curious as to what that gate really was.
800989: "That he died like a sausage?! What else can I tell his family!?" Either way, your volunteer leapt through the fire and paid with his life. Who knows — perhaps dousing his mantlecoat in a protective layer of paraffin was a mistake! Your expedition will have to trudge the miserable way round.
800990: The crew have no regrets in plotting what they perceive to be a safer, more rational course. Sweaty jungles are the devil they know, snakes and spiders notwithstanding. They make good time, and soon find a shallow incline that leads them up and over to the far side of the ridge. Still, many are curious to know what sorcery was governing the gate they saw.
800991: The jungle thins out to a precipice, which seems to form part of the ridge you are trying to cross. A long and shoddy-looking bridge stretches to the other side, if you want to risk it, or else you could attempt to take an even larger detour.
800992: There is no way through, thanks to your shambolic map reading, as the jungle grows thicker and danker. The group tire, having many disagreements, and separate into factions. The sensible ones stick together, and decide the only realistic option is to backtrack for several weeks. The rest will die among the roots and ferns.
800995: Inspection shows it to be in passable condition. There are a few nerve-wracking moments during the crossing, as the wind whips up and the rickety bridge begins to sway. In any case, all are rather pleased to reach the other side, from which they succeed in reaching the far side of the ridge.
800996: Only a fool would ever set foot on it! Of course, it's nothing if not dramatic as the bridge cables twang, and one after the other, your men pile into the gorge. The craftsmen who had been so very confident in the deathtrap structure's safety choose hang back in shame, as the expedition sorrowfully wends the long way round the ridge.
800997: It is a long trek, yet one that could have been so much longer were it not for some sound map reading and compass work. The vegetation is thick and stubborn. Your expedition hacks their way through with irritation, marking yet another hiccup for the expedition log book.
800998: Imbecile orienteers! There's no way to cross this river valley for a hundred miles! You've covered half that distance before you realise, but having wasted a lot of time and provisions, your men may as well see this major boo-boo through. It takes almost three weeks of struggle before your expedition is back on track.
801002: The discovery of several strange artefacts aboard spooks the crew. Tied to the rigging, bunks, boards, and even atop the captain's desk. A warning, a threat? And who put them there? Since the nearby island is uninhabited, it is sensible only to think the perpetrator must be aboard. The crew must know or have seen something last night!
801004: Ask the crew who did this
801005: Throw them overboard and move on.
801006: 'For good luck,' remarks the anthropologist, inspecting the spherical red dolls, 'for the setting of goals, and perseverance in achieving them. Some people or spirit of this place believe they can help us home.' At this, your crew are beguiled.
801007: Your crew are beginning to bond. Someone comes forward, not having expected to cause such a bother. 'They're for me old mum,' he sighs, 'birds - that one's a little robin. 801008: No one has anything to offer but the priest. It is his belief that some unholy chapter has opened. The next morning, more of the eerie things have appeared. 'Cleanse the idols in holy fire!' he shrieks. 'Nonsense,' says a soldier. "Set guards within, and we shall have this rat."
801009: A destructive episode. No one has information, or perhaps they withhold it. Consensus tends towards the latter. Someone wants this expedition to fail, and these effigies are a threat. Paranoia festers. At the next port, a large part of the crew opts to quit.
801010: Chilling. As instructed, the crew collect the dolls and throw them overboard. But relief lasts only until the following morning, when the dolls are found returned, placed exactly as they had been.
801011: Side with the priest and prepare a holy fire
801012: Keep guard and capture the perpetrator
801013: The priest gloats over his success. With a maniacal grin, he sets the mound of idols alight. The fire consumes rapidly, shifting vermillion to viridian. Some say they hear the wood scream as it goes. 'Expurgation is God's work, and I am chosen.'
801014: The fire is chaotic, and the buckets of water seem not to extinguish, but provoke. The flame leaps to the priest's cassock like spring-heeled jack, and as it sweeps up his back, he is heard to utter his last words, 'forgive me father, for I have sinned.'
801015: The teenagers are remorseful. 'It was a jape, a piece o' trickery sirs, we regret t'were not received so.' The crew are forgiving - the youths merely wished to contain their homesickness - and call for just fifty strokes of the birch per bottom.
801016: That night, dire musket-shot is heard. A dead boy on deck, local. A second is seen diving to blue. Next morning a rhythm comes from an armada of river boats, armed with guns. There island is inhabited, and they know what you have done.
801017: The sun is solemn that morning. The bodies of the dead guards are borne to the hold for burial, but not here, upon this cursed rock. Who killed them none know but the sinister effigies. The expedition fumbles on.
801020: One warning salvo is enough. The river boats cluster and slow. Though they lower their weapons and allow you to leave, the anger that your crime goes unpunished couldn't be more marked in their faces.
801021: Your ship is a sitting duck. Your crew cannot man stations fast enough to fire or manoeuvre. Enemy boats surround your ship, before scaling its sides. The blood shed on both sides will stain this ship and expedition forever.
801022: Once your ship is underway she is free. Nevertheless your adversaries are excellent shots, and do damage to the sails and aft. The crew will have to make repairs in the days that follow.
801023: A traumatic escape. In the hurry to leave, your ship is spun broadside and exposed to gunfire. There are injuries, but none so deep as the sight of the dead boy's accomplice below. He weeps, and clutches one of the idols - a good luck charm.
801026: Robbed! Having thanked the generous innkeeper, your ship departed what seemed a most hospitable port. Even at the time, your crew were surprised to see so many smiling faces gather at the dock to wave you off. A mere hour into the onward journey, however, it's discovered that a great deal of valuable property is missing from the hold. You must now decide if it's worth going back for.
801029: Return to the inn in disguise and bait the robbers
801031: Take the loss on the chin
801032: The detective already knows the culprit. "I was waiting to see if our crew were complicit, but I am satisfied they are not." Your ship returns and lays out a watertight case to the local authorities, incriminating the local innkeeper. He is arrested, your equipment is returned and your ship receives a resupply. It seems that hospitality was genuine after all!
801033: Swift justice. The petty harbour defences crumble in the morning light. Your ship streaks unopposed into what remains of the smouldering harbour, and turns its guns upon the harbourmaster's office. "Please, take anything!" he yelps, "You'll find all your things in the warehouse, and more besides." You profit from a scheme that has been running for years.
801034: Your assault is too slow. Just as you begin to gain the upper hand over the defenders, the cavalry appear. Cannons pop from the west; a slew of artillery reinforcements.
801035: An absolute shambles. Your men couldn't even best a few locals with a primitive demi-cannon. "Who shall have our guts for garters next?" yelp those who survive the barrage, "A small gang of angry turtles?" Your ship sails hurriedly away.
801037: You put an end to the corruption! Brought to their knees, the local authorities admit a conspiracy in which all were complicit. "It was never meant to go this far. 801038: The enemy force is vast. "There's too many, Captain! We must turn back!" But it is too late. The western cliff lights up with cannon fire, and your ship follows suit. Many lives will be lost before you finally crawl out of range.
801039: Make peace, and reason with the officials
801040: Despite your earlier aggression, they are willing to listen. After an exasperating few days, you are finally able to prove your losses. The authorities take in any dockers who are found to be guilty, and most, if not all of your possessions are returned.
801041: The authorities stand with their own. Following a ceasefire, you make your case as best you can, but it's not enough. Furthermore, you must answer for the damage you've caused. Unfortunately, this will mean leaving some of your best sailors behind to help with repairs.
801042: You rumble the schemers! The crew set aside superstition, and paint the ship with a different name.
